course_details.Overview of class: The Elementary First-year course, French 111-2, is the second quarter of a three-quarter course for students with no previous study of French, or with less than one year of High School French. Classes meet three times a week (MWF) with additional asynchronous work. Please note, students cannot audit 100-level language courses, or take these courses for P/PN, and must earn a C- or better to advance to the next course in the sequence.
course_details.Registration Requirements: French 111-1, placement by the Northwestern Online French Placement Test (https://placement.madstudio.northwestern.edu/), or permission from the Department. If students have studied French for more than one year in High School, they must take the Northwestern Online French Placement Test to determine if they qualify for a more advanced course (such as the intensive First-year course, French 115). For students to receive credit for French 111-2, they must: 1) take the online Placement Test and be placed into French 111-2, or 2) receive permission from the French 111 course coordinator to enroll in the course. If neither case is true, students will not receive credit for this course.
course_details.Learning Objectives: Students develop speaking, listening, reading and writing skills at the intermediate level of French in a cultural context and foster critical thinking.
course_details.Teaching Method: Class sessions will include a variety of communicative activities designed to help students develop their knowledge of basic French vocabulary and structures along with the ability to use what they have learned. Classes will be conducted exclusively in French except when explanation of grammar or other material may necessitate the use of English. Students are expected to prepare outside of class, to participate actively in class activities, and to work independently with the En Avant! online learning platform: Connect.
course_details.Evaluation Method: Final grades are based on class participation and attendance, homework, compositions, quizzes, written exams, and oral assessments.
course_details.Class Materials (Required): French 111-1, French 111-2, and French 111-3 will use the following textbook: En Avant! 4th edition: (with Connect access code). https://www.mheducation.com/highered/product/en-avant-beginning-french-student-edition-anderson-dolidon/M9781259999826.html#buying-options. You will need to purchase the FOURTH edition - you MUST have access to Connect.
course_details.Class Notes: Students may contact Student Services Enrichment Office (https://www.northwestern.edu/enrichment) for help and information about low-cost options for textbooks.

course_details.Overview of class: The intensive First-year course, French 115-2, is the second of a two-quarter sequence (Fall and Winter quarters) is designed for students who have studied French for more than one year in High School or in another context. This course covers the same material as the three-quarter sequence of French 111. Classes meet three times a week (MWF) with additional asynchronous work. The aim of the course is to review and develop skills in speaking, understanding, reading, writing and cultural competence. Please note, students cannot audit 100-level language courses, or take these courses for P/PN, and must earn a C- or better to advance to the next course in the sequence.
course_details.Registration Requirements: French 115-1, placement by the Northwestern Online French Placement Test (https://placement.madstudio.northwestern.edu/), or permission from the Department. If students have studied French for more than one year in High School, have not taken the online Placement Test and/or have not received permission from the course coordinator to enroll in French 115-2, they will not receive credit for this course.

course_details.Teaching Method: Class sessions will include a variety of communicative activities designed to help students develop their knowledge of basic French vocabulary and structures along with the ability to use what they have learned. Classes will be conducted exclusively in French except when explanation of grammar or other material may necessitate the use of English. Students are expected to prepare outside of class, to participate actively in class activities, and to work independently with the En Avant! online learning platform: Connect.
course_details.Evaluation Method: Final grades are based on class participation and attendance, homework, compositions, quizzes, written exams, a final creative project, and a final oral exam.

course_details.Overview of class: French 121-2 is the second quarter of a three-quarter course for students who have completed French 121-1 or have been placed in this course after taking the Placement test of the Department of French and Italian. The primary goal of this course is to strengthen oral and written communication skills by immersing students in authentic cultural contexts and language. A review of essential grammar and vocabulary will reinforce linguistic foundations. Classes meet three times a week (MWF) with one day of additional asynchronous work. Please note, students cannot audit 100-level language courses, or take these courses for P/PN, and must earn a C- or better to advance to the next course in the sequence.
course_details.Registration Requirements: French 121-1 or placement by the Northwestern Online French Placement Test (https://placement.madstudio.northwestern.edu).
course_details.Learning Objectives: Students develop speaking, listening, reading and writing skills at the intermediate level of French in a cultural context and foster critical thinking.
course_details.Teaching Method: Class activities are devoted to conversation and communicative activities that will allow students to practice what they have learned while exploring contemporary French and Francophone cultures. Classes will be conducted exclusively in French except when explanation of grammar or other material may necessitate the use of English. Students are expected to prepare outside of class, to participate actively in class activities, and to work independently with the pioneering courseware developed by faculty in the French Department at Northwestern.
course_details.Evaluation Method: Students will be evaluated on class participation, oral and written homework, unit tests, and an end-of-quarter project.
course_details.Class Materials (Required): The courseware available through Canvas at no cost. Talk Abroad fee for conversations with native speakers: around $30 (students may contact the coordinator for other options).

Attendance at 1st class mandatory
Prerequisites apply, see description

course_details.Overview of class:
On September 4, 2026, the UN General Assembly voted overwhelmingly in favor of a new world map in which Africa will be depicted more accurately. Current world maps, based on what is called the "Mercator Projection," from 1569, devised for navigation, shrink land masses closest to the equator. This debate reminds us that decolonization is an active and ongoing process not only historically and politically but also epistemologically, that is including the shifting status of our knowledge. Maps, creations at the intersection of science, history, imagination, and ideology, are not mere representations of the world. Rather, more actively, they configure our position relative to the world and our ideas of it. They are texts that are read and interpreted and thus part and parcel of how power relations are discursively constituted and maintained. For this reason, cartography is a central element in both colonization and decolonization.

This course introduces students to key anticolonial and decolonizing works by Francophone African and Caribbean writers and thinkers by beginning with how these regions were mapped. Following a visit to the Herskovits Library of African Studies map collection, we will turn to V. Y. Mudimbe's influential work to understand how "Africa" is foremost a discursive formation; an imagined and invented idea with a long and complex history, rather than a merely natural and self-evident geographical mass. We will expand upon these insights by reading works by Caribbean and African thinkers on colonization's long history, and the diversity of their ideas about what it means to decolonize across generations. Because many of these thinkers are also poets and writers of fiction, our readings will include philosophical, historical, and literary works to explore differences in forms of expression. The course aims to show both the robustness of this complex critical tradition and its shifting and diverse orientations.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
• Apply the techniques of close reading to a wide array of texts (philosophical, historical, literary, and visual).
• Understand the political and ethical value of thinking about the past for the present.
• Understand the relation between history, politics, knowledge, and the imagination in shaping our understanding of our world.
• Develop oral ability to analyze texts and communicate ideas clearly and concisely.
• Hone writing skill by organizing ideas and arguments in a coherent and persuasive manner.
• Learn to generate thoughtful questions based on the materials studied in class.
• Challenge thoughtfully and carefully the ideas and assumptions of others as well as their own.

course_details.Overview of class:
This course offers the students the opportunity to discover the influential work of the renowned Moroccan thinker and writer, Abdelkebir Khatibi. An innovative writer, philosopher, essayist, and poet, the significance of Khatibi's thought on contemporary decolonial thought across disciplines, notably sociology, anthropology, political, literary and aesthetics cannot be overestimated. While much of his theoretical insights are based in the history and aesthetic cultures of Morocco, his concepts and methodologies have given new and nuanced breath to how scholars think, write, and study non-Western histories and cultures. His novel Amour bilingue as well as his collections of essays collected in Maghreb Pluriel and La blessure du nom propre are today necessary references for all serious students and scholars of postcolonial and decolonial thought.

In this course, we will begin by first historicizing the Maghreb (Francophone North Africa) as a geographical, historical, and political configuration in order to understand the background of some of Khatibi's thinking. We will then read several essays and two novels, and autobiography by Khatibi and will consult some helpful critical readings on his key notions. The aim of the course is to familiarize students with one of the leading voices in contemporary debates in postcolonial and decolonial studies.

course_details.Overview of class: Sailors played a paradoxical role in European imperial projcts in the modern period. On the one hand, they were the agents of empire, spreading European civilization throughout the world. On the other, they were often drawn from the lower classes of society, and, in the case of France, from Brittany, a region of France that was itself a kind of colonized space, where residents mostly spoke Breton rather than French. The sailor was also closely associated with supposedly asocial behaviors: criminality, same-sex sexuality, rampant non-monogamous heterosexuality, and interracial relationships. In this class, we will explore these paradoxes of the figure of the sailor in French literature and film of the 19th and 20th centuries, through the works of Melville, Pierre Loti, Joseph Conrad, Jean Cocteau, RW Fassbinder, and Claire Denis.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
Literature and Arts
In this course, students will learn to:
● Observe the forms of expression, in words, images, cultural and everyday practices by
way of close analysis.
● Gain awareness of the philosophical, cultural, and historical factors influencing the
problematic we are studying in our course.
● Appreciate how the works we read across various historical periods and cultural and
political landscapes reveal the differences and diversities as well as the continuity and
unity of questions about human culture and thought.
● Enhance the skills of literary and cultural interpretation, analysis, and commentary,
spoken, visual and written.
● Develop writing and oral skills by sharpening powers of interpretation, critique, and
aesthetic perception.
● Enlarge your conceptual vocabulary to understand and express abstract notions.
Global Overlay
In this course, students will learn to:
● Engage with visual, literary and cultural works to reflect on global intercultural relations
among groups, cultural traditions, and/or nations, in French and Francophone contexts.
● Explore the social, political, historical, and cultural bases of identity, be it national,
regional, racial, culture, and how they constitute themselves and are constituted by
others.
● Understand how such differences as race, class, ethnicity, gender, and sexual
orientation are historically contingent and participate in the construction of otherness
and sameness.
● Analyze the key issue of colonialism.
Advanced Expression
The written and oral assignments in this course serve to:
● Focus on effective communication, be it through writing, speaking or other modes of
communication, in specific disciplinary or interdisciplinary contexts.
● Understand and emulate field-specific conventions and protocols for communicating
findings to a range of audiences.
● Develop the relationship between their voice and field-specific norms of expression,
aiming to achieve control over persuasive rhetoric.
● Pay attention to style, precision of language, the nature and potential of words for
thinking.
● Develop an individual style of argumentation and presentation of research.

course_details.Overview of class: In this course, students revise and expand a paper written in a previous course with the aim of producing an article manuscript of approximately 20-25 pages in length and submitting it for publication upon completion of the seminar. In the revised article, students develop an original argument relative to a significant problem or research question; demonstrate knowledge of relevant primary and secondary sources and the ability to evaluate them critically; engage with an appropriate theoretical or scholarly methodology; and draw out clearly the significance of their findings. The class meets regularly as a group for the purpose of discussion and feedback on individual work. Students submit written assignments and make short presentations on essential elements of their articles, including the argument, the current state of the secondary research, and their contribution to the field. In addition, they receive and write a reader's report similar to those generated by referees of journal submissions. Throughout the course, students will meet individually with the professor to discuss their progress in addition to working with their peers. Work written or revised over the course of the quarter will be shared and discussed in the final class meeting. This course is required for 2nd and 3rd year graduate students in French. It will be taught in English and is open to graduate students in other programs.
course_details.Learning Objectives: The main goal of the course is to enable the student to submit an article for publication by the end of the term. Students will become familiar with styles of academic writing, conventions of scholarly publication and peer review, strategies for devising and following through with a feasible study, and the process of finding a journal that is appropriate to their writing style, topic, and theoretical/methodological interests. They will be supported in developing their own voice and articulating the major contribution of their work.
